newsitem.title: UK: UK government concerned about alcoholic soft drinks.
newsitem.headline: UK government concerned about alcoholic soft drinks.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government said on Friday it will study the problems caused by "alcopops" -- fruit favoured alcoholic drinks -- amid growing concern they are a prime cause of drunkenness and crime among teenagers.
Interior minister Jack Straw said he had asked a team of junior ministers to "consider what further action may be necessary to stop this abuse developing".
Straw said in a statement: "We all know the links between alcohol abuse and crime. Everything must be done to stop young people falling into a downward spiral of offending."

Alcopops, marketed in brightly-labelled bottles under names such as Hooch, Lemonhead and Diamond Zest, and stronger than most beers sold in bars, have become popular in Britain following their launch in 1995. Sales are now worth 265 million pounds ($433.5 million) a year.

They are increasingly blamed for an rise in drinking among young people barely, or even not yet, in their teens although the leading producers say they are aimed at people over the legal age for drinking in pubs of 18.

A judge in Bolton, northern England, on Thursday attacked their makers as "grossly irresponsible" after hearing that a 14-year-old boy who got drunk on alcopops had started a school blaze, causing 750,000 pounds ($1.23 million) of damage.
The tabloid Sun newspaper devoted 1-1/2 pages to the problem on Friday. Its survey of 700 14- to 17-year olds found that all but six percent drank some form of alcohol and 59 percent drank alcopops.
"The drinks are marketed to them despite what the industry claims," the paper said in an editorial. "Our family man Prime Minister (Tony Blair) should act quickly."
